definitions.text: To deprive of sacramental character or efficacy; as, to unsacrament the rite of baptism. [Obs.]
Unsteady; fickle. [Obs.] O, stormy people, unsad and ever untrue. Chaucer.
To relieve from sadness; to cheer. [R.] Whitlock.
To strip of a saddle; to take the saddle from, as a horse.
To throw from the saddle; to unhorse.
Infirmity; weakness. [Obs.] Wyclif.
The quality or state of being in peril; absence of safety; insecurity. Bacon.
To deprive of saintship; to deny sanctity to. [R.] South.
Unbecoming to a saint. Gauden.
Not salable; unmerchantable.
That which can not be sold. Byron.
Absence or lack of sanctification. Shak.
Quality of being unsatiable; insatiability. [Obs.]
Insatiable. [Obs.] Hooker.
Insatiate. Dr. H. More.
Dissatisfaction. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
Capable of absorbing or dissolving to a greater degree; as, an unsaturated solution.
(Chem.)
Capable of taking up, or of uniting with, certain other elements or compounds, without the elimination of any side product; thus, aldehyde, ethylene, and ammonia are unsaturated.
The quality or state of being unsaturated.
To recant or recall, as what has been said; to refract; to take back again; to make as if not said. You can say and unsay things at pleasure. Goldsmith.
To divest of scales; to remove scales from. [An eagle] purging and unscaling her long-abused sight at the fountain itself of heavenly radiance. Milton.
Not be escaped; inevitable. [Obs.] Wyclif.
Etym: [Pref. un- not + sceptered.]
Having no scepter.
Etym: [1st pref. un- + scepter.]
Deprived of a scepter.
Etym: [Pref. un- not + sceptered.]
Having no scepter.
Etym: [1st pref. un- + scepter.]
Deprived of a scepter.
Want of science or knowledge; ignorance. [Obs.] If that any wight ween a thing to be otherwise than it is, it is not only unscience, but it is deceivable opinion. Chaucer.
To draw the screws from; to loose from screws; to loosen or withdraw (anything, as a screw) by turning it.
Not scrupulous; unprincipled.
Inscrutable. [R.]
Destitute of an escutcheon. [R.] Pollock.
To break or remove the seal of; to open, as what is sealed; as, to unseal a letter. Unable to unseal his lips beyond the width of a quarter of an inch. Sir W. Scott.
To disclose, as a secret. [Obs.] The Coronation.
To open the seam or seams of; to rip; to cut; to cut open. Shak.
Not searchable; inscrutable; hidden; mysterious. The counsels of God are to us unsearchable. Rogers.
To make unseasoned; to deprive of seasoning.
To strike unseasonably; to affect disagreeably or unfavorably. Why do I send this rustic madrigal, That may thy tuneful ear unseason quite Spenser.

Not seasonable; being, done, or occurring out of the proper season; ill-timed; untimely; too early or too late; as, he called at an unseasonable hour; unseasonable advice; unseasonable frosts; unseasonable food.
Not seasoned.
Untimely; ill-timed. [Obs.] Shak.
To throw from one's seat; to deprive of a seat. Cowper.
Specifically, to deprive of the right to sit in a legislative body, as for fraud in election. Macaulay.
Not seconded; not supported, aided, or assisted; as, the motion was unseconded; the attempt was unseconded.
Not exemplified a second time. [Obs.] "Strange and unseconded shapes of worms." Sir T. Browne.
To disclose; to divulge. [Obs.] Bacon.
Not secret; not close; not trusty; indiscreet. [Obs.] "We are unsecret to ourselves." Shak.
To cause to become not secular; to detach from secular things; to alienate from the world.
Insecure. [R.] Milton.
To open, as the eyes of a hawk that have been seeled; hence, to give light to; to enlighten. [Obs.] B. Jonson.
Not to seem. [Obs.] Shak.
Unbeseeming; not fit or becoming.
The quality or state of being unseemly; unbecomingness. Udall.
Not seemly; unbecoming; indecent. An unseemly outbreak of temper. Hawthorne.
In an unseemly manner.
Not seen or discovered.
Unskilled; inexperienced. [Obs.] Clarendon.
Not seldom; frequently. [R.]
Not blessed or happy; wretched; unfortunate. [Written also unsilly.] [Obs.] Chaucer.
Deprived of virility, or seminal energy; made a eunuch. [Obs.]
Wanting a distinct meaning; having no certain signification. [R.] Puller.
Insensible. [Obs.]
To elevate from the domain of the senses; to purify. Coleridge.
Inseparable. [Obs.] "In love unseparable." Shak.
Neglect of duty; idleness; indolence. [Obs.] Massinger.
Not set; not fixed or appointed.
To move or loosen from a settled position or state; to unfix; to displace; to disorder; to confuse.
To become unsettled or unfixed; to be disordered. Shak.
The quality or state of being unsettled.
The act of unsettling, or state of being unsettled; disturbance. J. H. Newman.
To render other than seven; to make to be no longer seven. [Obs. & R.] "To unseven the sacraments of the church of Rome." Fuller.
To undo, as something sewn, or something inclosed by sewing; to rip apart; to take out the stitches of.
To deprive of sex, or of qualities becoming to one's sex; esp., to make unfeminine in character, manners, duties, or the like; as, to unsex a woman.
Not sexual; not proper or peculiar to one of the sexes. De Quincey.
To loose from shackles or bonds; to set free from restraint; to unfetter. Addison.
Not capable of being shaken; firm; fixed. Shak. J. S. Mill.
Unshaken. [Obs.] Shak.
To strip the shale, or husk, from; to uncover. [Obs.] I will not unshale the jest before it be ripe. Marston.
To deprive of shape, or of proper shape; to disorder; to confound; to derange. [R.] Shak.
Not shaped; shapeless; misshapen; deformed; ugly.
Not shaped; shapeless; misshapen; deformed; ugly.
To deprive of a sheath; to draw from the sheath or scabbard, as a sword. To unsheathe the sword, to make war.
Not parted or divided, as the hair. [Obs.] Spenser.
Not spilt, or made to flow, as blood or tears. Milton.
To strip the shell from; to take out of the shell; to hatch.
To remove from, or as from, a shelf.
Not shent; not disgraced; blameless. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
To depose from the office of sheriff. [R.]
To unshut. [Obs.] Chaucer.
That may
Shiftless; helpless. [Obs.]
To take out of a ship or vessel; as, to unship goods.
(Naut.)
To remove or detach, as any part or implement, from its proper position or connection when in use; as, to unship an oar; to unship capstan bars; to unship the tiller.
The act of unshipping, or the state of being unshipped; displacement.
To remove the shot from, as from a shotted gun; to unload.
Not hit by a shot; also, not discharged or fired off.
To recall what is done by shouting. [Obs.] Shak.
To remove the shroud from; to uncover. P. Fletcher.
Being without shrubs.
To open, or throw open. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To open or remove the shutters of. T. Hughes.

Doing or done without sight; not seeing or examining. [Colloq.] Unsight unseen, a colloquial phrase, denoting unseeing unseen, or unseen repeated; as, to buy a thing unsight unseen, that is, without seeing it. For to subscribe, unsight, unseen, To a new church discipline. Hudibras. There was a great confluence of chapmen, that resorted from every part, with a design to purchase, which they were to do "unsight unseen." Spectator.
Invisible. [Obs.]
Not sighted, or seen. Suckling.
(Gun.)
Not aimed by means of a sight; also, not furnished with a sight, or with a properly adjusted sight; as, to shoot and unsighted rife or cannon.
Insignificant. [Obs.] Holland.
See Unsely. [Obs.]
Absence of simplicity; artfulness. C. Kingsley.
To deprive of sinfulness, as a sin; to make sinless. [Obs.] Feltham.
Not sincere or pure; insincere. [Obs.] Dryden.
The quality or state of being unsincere or impure; insincerity.
To deprive of sinews or of strength. [R.] Dryden.
To separate, as sisters; to disjoin. [Poetic & R.] Tennyson.
Not sisterly. Richardson.
Unresisting. [Obs.] "The unsisting postern." Shak.
Not sitting well; unbecoming. [Obs.] "Unsitting words." Sir T. More.
Want of skill; ignorance; unskillfulness. [Obs.] Sylvester.
Not skillful; inexperienced; awkward; bungling; as, an unskillful surgeon or mechanic; an unskillful logician.
Lacking discernment; injudicious; ignorant. Though it make the unskillful laugh, can not but make the judicious grieve. Shak.
Not slacked; unslaked; as, unslacked lime.
Not slaked; unslacked; as, an unslaked thirst; unslaked lime.
To take off the slings of, as a yard, a cask, or the like; to release from the slings. Totten.
To sluice; to open the sluice or sluices of; to let flow; to discharge. Dryden.
The quality or state of being unsociable; unsociableness.
Not sociable; not inclined to society; averse to companionship or conversation; solitary; reserved; as, an unsociable person or temper.
To loose or take from a socket.
Not soft; hard; coarse; rough. [Obs.] "Bristles of his beard unsoft." Chaucer.
Not softly. [Obs.] Great climbers fall unsoft. Spenser.
To separate or disunite, as what has been soldered; hence, to divide; to sunder. [Formerly written also unsoder.] Tennyson.
Not equipped like a soldier; unsoldierlike. [Obs.] J. Fletcher.
To divest of solemnity.
Incapable of being sounded. [Obs.]
Not soncy (sonsy); not fortunate. [Scot.]
Not sweet. [Obs.] Spenser.
Not sophisticated; pure; innocent; genuine.
Not sophisticated; pure; innocent; genuine.
Not sorrowed for; unlamented. Beau. & Fl.
Not sorted; not classified; as, a lot of unsorted goods.
Not well selected; ill-chosen. The purpose you undertake is dangerous; the friends you named uncertain; the time itself unsorted. Shak.
To deprive of soul, spirit, or principle. [R.] Shelton.
Not sound; not whole; not solid; defective; infirm; diseased.
To take the spars, stakes, or bars from. [R.] Sir W. Scott.
Not sparing; not parsimonious; liberal; profuse. Burke.
Not merciful or forgiving. [R.] Milton.
To retract, as what has been spoken; to recant; to unsay. [R.] Shak.

Not speakable; incapable of being uttered or adequately described; inexpressible; unutterable; ineffable; as, unspeakable grief or rage. Ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory. 1 Pet. i. 8.
Not specialized; specifically (Biol.), not adapted, or set apart, for any particular purpose or function; as, an unspecialized unicellular organism. W. K. Brooks.
Not performed; not dispatched. [Obs.] Garth.
To break the power of (a spell); to release (a person) from the influence of a spell; to disenchant. [R.] Such practices as these, . . . The more judicious Israelites unspelled. Dryden.
To remove, as a planet, from its sphere or orb. Shak.
To remove a spike from, as from the vent of a cannon.
Not spilt or wasted; not shed.
To untwist, as something spun.
To dispirit. [Obs.] Sir W. Temple.
To deprive of spiritually. South.
Deprived of a spleen.
Not spotted; free from spot or stain; especially, free from moral stain; unblemished; immaculate; as, an unspotted reputation.
To divest of the title or privilege of an esquire. Swift.
Not stable; not firm, fixed, or constant; subject to change or overthrow. equilibrium, under Stable.
To remove, or take away, from a stack; to remove, as something constituting a stack.
To free from starch; to make limp or pliable.
To deprive of state or dignity. [R.] High-battled Cæsar will unstate his happiness. Shak.
To disarm; to soften. Richardson.
To remove, as a mast, from its step.
To release, as one thing stuck to another. Richardson.
Not still; restless. [R.]
To disarm of a sting; to remove the sting of. [R.] "Elegant dissertations on virtue and vice . . . will not unsting calamity." J. M. Mason.
To open by picking out stitches; to take out, or undo, the stitches of; as, to unstitch a seam. Collier.
To deprive of a stock; to remove the stock from; to loose from that which fixes, or holds fast.
To remove from the stocks, as a ship.
Etym: [Pref. un- not + stocking.]
Destitute of stockings. Sir W. Scott.
Etym: [1st pref. un- + stocking.]
Deprived of stockings.
To take the stopple or stopper from; as, to unstop a bottle or a cask.
To free from any obstruction; to open.
To relieve from a strain; to relax. B. Jonson.
Not strained; not cleared or purified by straining; as, unstrained oil or milk.
Not forced; easy; natural; as, a unstrained deduction or inference. Hakewill.
Not stratified; -- applied to massive rocks, as granite, porphyry, etc., and also to deposits of loose material, as the glacial till, which occur in masses without layers or strata.
Want of strength; weakness; feebleness. [Obs.] Wyclif.
Nonstriated; unstriped.
To deprive of a string or strings; also, to take from a string; as, to unstring beads.
To loosen the string or strings of; as, to unstring a harp or a bow.
To relax the tension of; to loosen. "His garland they unstring." Dryden.
Used also figuratively; as, his nerves were unstrung by fear.
Not striped.
(Nat. Hist.)
Without marks or striations; nonstriated; as, unstriped muscle fibers.
Not studied; not acquired by study; unlabored; natural.
Not skilled; unversed; -- followed by in.
Not spent in study. [Obs.] "To cloak the defects of their unstudied years." Milton.
Lacking in matter or substance; visionary; chimerical.
To make unsubstantial. [R.]
A divesting of substantiality.
Not able or likely to succeed. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.
Want of success; failure; misfortune. Prof. Wilson.
Not successful; not producing the desired event; not fortunate; meeting with, or resulting in, failure; unlucky; unhappy.
Insufferable. [Obs.] Hooker.
Inability or incapability of enduring, or of being endured.
Insufficiency. [Obs.] Hooker.
Insufficiency. [Obs.] Hooker.
Insufficient. [Obs.]
Not to suit; to be unfit for. [Obs.] Quarles.
Insupportable; unendurable.
Not made sure. [Obs.] Thy now unsured assurance to the crown. Shak.
Want of surety; uncertainty; insecurity; doubt. [Obs.] Sir T. More.
Insurmountable. Locke.
The quality or state of being unsuspecting. Dickens.
To take a swaddle from; to unswathe.
To take a swathe from; to relieve from a bandage; to unswaddle. Addison.
Not capable of being swayed. Shak.
To recant or recall, as an oath; to recall after having sworn; to abjure. J. Fletcher.
To recall an oath. Spenser.
To relieve from perspiration; to ease or cool after exercise or toil. [R.] Milton.
To sink from a swollen state; to subside. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Wanting in symmetry, or due proportion pf parts.
(Biol.)
Not symmetrical; being without symmetry, as the parts of a flower when similar parts are of different size and shape, or when the parts of successive circles differ in number. See Symmetry.
(Chem.)

Being without symmetry of chemical structure or relation; as, an unsymmetrical carbon atom. Unsymmetrical carbon atom (Chem.), one which is united at once to four different atoms or radicals. This condition usually occasions physical isomerism, with the attendant action on polarized light.
Not symmetrically.
Absence or lack of sympathy.
